statements.quote: Modern AI is, at its core, applied linear algebra.
Every image, every word, every token lives in a high-dimensional **vector space**.
This chapter introduces the mathematical objects that make neural networks possible: vectors, matrices, tensors, and the operations that combine them.
If you complete this chapter, the rest of the textbook, embeddings, attention, gradients, activations, will read as natural applications of these primitives.
In 1D, you only have one “degree of freedom.” You can go forward or backward.
By adding a second number, we unlock an infinite flat surface.
\citealternativetitle{rgb_color_cube}: every color in this RGB color cube is a single point inside it, located by its Red, Green, and Blue coordinates.
In 3D, we can represent volume.
A great way to visualize this is **Color Space**.
Every color you see on this screen is just a vector in a 3D space where the axes are **Red**, **Green**, and **Blue**.
We cannot “see” 4D, but we can **describe** it.
In AI, dimensions are just “features.” Imagine we are describing a “Fruit.” We can use a 4D vector to describe:
Every fruit is now a point in a 4D “Fruit Space.”
Sweet: Sour: Firm: Seeds:

The geometric picture above is intuitive, but it hides a question: when we add a vector to a vector, or stretch a vector by a number, *what rules must those operations obey?* A **vector space** is the precise answer.
You don't need to memorise the eight axioms.
What you need to remember is:
**A vector is not a "list of numbers".** A vector is an *element* of a vector space.
The list-of-numbers representation only appears once you pick a basis — that is, once you choose how to measure vectors.
The vector itself exists without that choice.
(This is why we can rotate, stretch, or translate an embedding space in later chapters without changing the meaning of "vector".)
A **scalar** is a single number from the base field — in this course, almost always a real number.
You use scalars every time you stretch a vector or measure a single quantity.
A **vector** is an element of a vector space.

The geometric picture is an *arrow* with a direction and a length: "three steps to the right, four steps up." The algebraic picture is a single thing you can add to other vectors and stretch with scalars.
If you pick a basis, you can write a vector as a list of coordinates.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the standard basis (\cite[Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, §2B, p.
39]{axler2024linearalgebra}), the arrow "3 right, 4 up, 2 forward" becomes the column
Two important properties:
To make a color, a computer needs a list of 3 numbers: one for Red, one for Green, one for Blue.
This 3-tuple is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$:
A vector is *not glued to one spot*.
The arrow "3 right, 4 up" is the same arrow whether you draw it starting at the origin or somewhere else.
This is what it means for vectors to be *free* (not anchored to a point).
Vectors can have any number of dimensions.

Vectors can also be added:
A **Matrix** is a grid of numbers (like a spreadsheet).
A **Black & White photo** is just a Matrix.
Each spot in the grid tells the computer how bright that specific pixel is, when we say $0$ means “black”, $255$ means white and everything inbetween are different shades of gray.

Historically, a matrix began as a *bookkeeping device*: Sylvester's oblong array existed so that one could pick square sub-arrays and form determinants from them (\cite[Sylvester, 1850]{sylvester1850matrix}).
Cayley's 1858 memoir changed its status.

He defined addition, multiplication and inversion of matrices, checked that a $2\times2$ matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, and introduced the "transposed matrix" (\cite[Cayley, 1858]{cayleymemoirmatrices}).
A grid of numbers became an object with an algebra — the step that lets a neural network's weight matrix be multiplied, inverted and differentiated.
You have seen scalars, vectors, and matrices.

statements.quote: The same word — *tensor* — has a stricter meaning in mathematics and physics.
There, a tensor is *an element of a tensor product of vector spaces*, the object used in general relativity, electromagnetism, and continuum mechanics.
Its identity is fixed by **transformation rules**: how its components change under a change of coordinates is part of what the object *is*, not a property the array enforces.

A numpy array of numbers does not, by virtue of being a numpy array, satisfy the geometric axioms of a tensor — the array can store a tensor's components, but nothing in the array itself guarantees that those components transform correctly under a change of basis.
That constraint lives in the math the array is being used to represent, not in the array.

The two meanings are connected historically — the ML usage borrowed the name because the underlying data structures share algebraic properties with the mathematical objects — but they are not the same definition.
If you go on to read physics or differential geometry, you will encounter:
In that language, a vector field is a $(1, 0)$-tensor, a one-form (linear functional) is a $(0, 1)$-tensor, and a metric tensor is a symmetric $(0, 2)$-tensor.
None of this matters for the ML sense above — but it is why the word was tempting to borrow.
One warning about the word *rank*.
In this chapter, "rank 2" for a matrix means **tensor order** — the number of axes — not the matrix rank of linear algebra.
The matrix rank is the dimension of the column space, the size of the largest non-vanishing minor.

Frobenius isolated that invariant in his 1878 memoir on linear substitutions and used the German word *Rang* in an 1879 paper (\cite[Frobenius, 1878]{frobenius1878linear}; \cite[Frobenius, 1879]{frobenius1879differential}); Sylvester supplied the complementary notion of *nullity* in 1884 (\cite[MacTutor: Matrices and determinants]{mactutor_matrices_determinants}).
A $3\times5$ matrix can have matrix rank 3, even though it is a rank-2 tensor.
Throughout this course, "tensor" means "multidimensional array" (the ML sense).
When you type numbers into the grid, the computer organises them into a structured object.

Each word is old, and each was coined to solve a concrete problem.
- **Matrix** — from Latin *mātrix*, "womb or mold," ultimately *māter*, "mother" \cite[matrix, Etymonline]{etymonline_matrix}.

Sylvester's problem was bookkeeping: building the invariant theory of eliminants, he needed a way to line up a determinant's terms so he could juggle them, and in 1850 he called the result a *matrix* — "a Matrix out of which we may form various systems of determinants" (\cite[Sylvester, 1850]{sylvester1850matrix}).

Cayley's problem was different: he wanted linear transformations to behave like numbers you can multiply and compose, and his 1858 "arithmetic of matrices" gave them exactly that (\cite[Cayley, 1858]{cayleymemoirmatrices}).
- **Vector** — from Latin *vĕctōr*, "a carrier," from *vĕhĕre*, "to carry" \cite[vector, Etymonline]{etymonline_vector}.

Hamilton wanted to do 3-D geometry the way complex numbers do 2-D: a "calculus of direction" that adds and rotates directed line segments in space without writing out every component (\cite[Hamilton, 1854]{hamiltonextensionsquaternions}).
- **Scalar** — from Latin *scalaris*, "of a ladder" (*scala*, a single step) \cite[scalar, Etymonline]{etymonline_scalar}.

It is Hamilton's word for the direction-free *amount* of a quantity — the part you can add and multiply like an ordinary number, split off from the direction a *vector* carries (\cite[Hamilton, 1854]{hamiltonextensionsquaternions}).
- **A note on the dates** — Hamilton pairs *scalar* and *vector* explicitly in his 1846 *Philosophical Magazine* paper: "the algebraically real part ...
the scalar" and the imaginary part "may be called the vector part" (\cite[Hamilton, 1846]{hamilton1846quaternions}).
The word *vector* itself is older — astronomers spoke of a *radius vector* — but Hamilton gave it the algebraic sense used here (\cite[Miller: vector]{miller_vector}).
- **Tensor** — the English word dates to 1704, a Modern Latin agent noun from *tendere*, "to stretch" \cite[tensor, Etymonline]{etymonline_tensor}.
Hamilton gave it a mathematical life, using it for the length of a quaternion.

The modern object had to solve Voigt's problem: a crystal's properties depend on the direction you probe them (stiffness, light, heat flow), and he needed one object to hold all those directional couplings — his "Tensoren," 1898 (\cite[Voigt, 1898]{voigt1898krystalle}).

Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita then built the calculus that makes tensors work, 1900, so that the laws of geometry could be written with no privileged coordinate system — the language Einstein inherited for relativity (\cite[Ricci-Curbastro & Levi-Civita, 1900]{riccilevicivita1900}; \cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).

- **Summation convention** — Einstein's 1916 answer to the tedium of long sums in his new tensor equations: an index that appears twice is summed over and then vanishes from the page (\cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).
Two details sharpen that story.

Voigt's word is not a definition of the modern tensor: he writes that he will call "die für sie charakteristischen physikalischen Grössen aber Tensoren" — the physical quantities characteristic of anisotropic crystals, "tensors" (\cite[Voigt, 1898]{voigt1898krystalle}).

And Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita's 1900 memoir does not use the noun at all; it speaks of *systèmes* with covariant and contravariant components (\cite[Ricci-Curbastro & Levi-Civita, 1900]{riccilevicivita1900}; \cite[Miller: tensor]{miller_tensor}).
The noun travelled from Voigt's crystallography into Einstein's relativity; the calculus came from the Italians.

> **One idea, many names.** Determinants came first (Seki 1683, Leibniz 1693), matrices were named for bookkeeping (Sylvester 1850), matrix algebra arrived in 1858 (Cayley), and tensors travelled from quaternions (Hamilton 1846) through crystallography (Voigt 1898) into relativity (Einstein 1916).
The array is the modern container; the history is the set of problems it was built to hold.

The **Hadamard Product** ($\odot$) was introduced by \citeauthor{hadamardproduct} to study **singularities** in complex power series: the term-by-term product and the related **Hadamard multiplication theorem** belong to his 1899 *Acta Mathematica* paper \citetitle{hadamard1899series}.

It is defined for vectors as $\vec{a} \odot \vec{b} = (a_1 b_1, \dots, a_n b_n)^T$ — the coefficients are multiplied term by term — which is exactly what lets one predict the analytic continuation and boundaries of functions derived from known ones.
The history is a little more tangled than the name suggests.

Hadamard's 1892 thesis was about Taylor series and analytic continuation; the term-by-term product and its multiplication theorem belong to his 1899 *Acta Mathematica* paper (\cite[Hadamard, 1899]{hadamard1899series}).

For matrices the key result is Schur's: the Hadamard product of two positive-semidefinite matrices is positive-semidefinite, proved as Theorem VII of his 1911 paper (\cite[Schur, 1911]{schur1911bilinear}).
The name "Hadamard product" for the matrix operation was popularised by Paul Halmos, who recalled that John von Neumann suggested it (\cite[Hadamard product, Wikipedia]{hadamard_product_wiki}).
While standard matrix multiplication follows the “row-by-column” rule, the **Hadamard Product** (also known as the *element-wise product*) is much more straightforward.
It takes two matrices or vectors of the **same dimensions** and multiplies the elements that occupy the same position.
In the context of Deep Learning, the $\odot$ symbol is ubiquitous.

It is used in **Layer Normalization** to scale normalized values by a learnable parameter $\gamma$, and in **Gating Mechanisms** (like LSTMs or GRUs) to decide which information should pass through a “gate.”
Adjust the values in vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ to see how the resulting vector is calculated element-by-element.
A matrix compounded with the transposed matrix gives rise to a symmetrical matrix.
Two vector operations appear so often in AI that they deserve explicit definitions here, even though they are first motivated in the Statistics and Loss chapters.
Given a vector of real-valued scores $\vec{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ (called **logits**), the **softmax** turns it into a vector of probabilities that sum to $1$:
The formula is older than machine learning.

It is the **Boltzmann distribution** of statistical mechanics — Boltzmann's 1868 paper, Gibbs's textbook of 1902 — with the logits playing the role of negative energies (\cite[Boltzmann distribution]{boltzmann_distribution_wiki}).
Duncan Luce derived it from his choice axiom in 1959 (\cite[Luce, 1959]{luce1959individualchoice}).
The name "softmax" is John Bridle's; he used it for a normalised exponential in a 1989 conference paper published in 1990 (\cite[Bridle, 1990]{bridle1990softmax}).

blocks.quote: A different word in mathematics

The same word — *tensor* — has a stricter meaning in mathematics and physics. There, a tensor is *an element of a tensor product of vector spaces*, the object used in general relativity, electromagnetism, and continuum mechanics. Its identity is fixed by **transformation rules**: how its components change under a change of coordinates is part of what the object *is*, not a property the array enforces. A numpy array of numbers does not, by virtue of being a numpy array, satisfy the geometric axioms of a tensor — the array can store a tensor's components, but nothing in the array itself guarantees that those components transform correctly under a change of basis. That constraint lives in the math the array is being used to represent, not in the array. The two meanings are connected historically — the ML usage borrowed the name because the underlying data structures share algebraic properties with the mathematical objects — but they are not the same definition.
If you go on to read physics or differential geometry, you will encounter:

In that language, a vector field is a $(1, 0)$-tensor, a one-form (linear functional) is a $(0, 1)$-tensor, and a metric tensor is a symmetric $(0, 2)$-tensor. None of this matters for the ML sense above — but it is why the word was tempting to borrow.

One warning about the word *rank*. In this chapter, "rank 2" for a matrix means **tensor order** — the number of axes — not the matrix rank of linear algebra. The matrix rank is the dimension of the column space, the size of the largest non-vanishing minor. Frobenius isolated that invariant in his 1878 memoir on linear substitutions and used the German word *Rang* in an 1879 paper (\cite[Frobenius, 1878]{frobenius1878linear}; \cite[Frobenius, 1879]{frobenius1879differential}); Sylvester supplied the complementary notion of *nullity* in 1884 (\cite[MacTutor: Matrices and determinants]{mactutor_matrices_determinants}). A $3\times5$ matrix can have matrix rank 3, even though it is a rank-2 tensor.
Throughout this course, "tensor" means "multidimensional array" (the ML sense).

Where the words come from
Each word is old, and each was coined to solve a concrete problem.

- **Matrix** — from Latin *mātrix*, "womb or mold," ultimately *māter*, "mother" \cite[matrix, Etymonline]{etymonline_matrix}. Sylvester's problem was bookkeeping: building the invariant theory of eliminants, he needed a way to line up a determinant's terms so he could juggle them, and in 1850 he called the result a *matrix* — "a Matrix out of which we may form various systems of determinants" (\cite[Sylvester, 1850]{sylvester1850matrix}). Cayley's problem was different: he wanted linear transformations to behave like numbers you can multiply and compose, and his 1858 "arithmetic of matrices" gave them exactly that (\cite[Cayley, 1858]{cayleymemoirmatrices}).

- **Vector** — from Latin *vĕctōr*, "a carrier," from *vĕhĕre*, "to carry" \cite[vector, Etymonline]{etymonline_vector}. Hamilton wanted to do 3-D geometry the way complex numbers do 2-D: a "calculus of direction" that adds and rotates directed line segments in space without writing out every component (\cite[Hamilton, 1854]{hamiltonextensionsquaternions}).

- **Scalar** — from Latin *scalaris*, "of a ladder" (*scala*, a single step) \cite[scalar, Etymonline]{etymonline_scalar}. It is Hamilton's word for the direction-free *amount* of a quantity — the part you can add and multiply like an ordinary number, split off from the direction a *vector* carries (\cite[Hamilton, 1854]{hamiltonextensionsquaternions}).

- **A note on the dates** — Hamilton pairs *scalar* and *vector* explicitly in his 1846 *Philosophical Magazine* paper: "the algebraically real part ... we shall call ... the scalar" and the imaginary part "may be called the vector part" (\cite[Hamilton, 1846]{hamilton1846quaternions}). The word *vector* itself is older — astronomers spoke of a *radius vector* — but Hamilton gave it the algebraic sense used here (\cite[Miller: vector]{miller_vector}).

- **Tensor** — the English word dates to 1704, a Modern Latin agent noun from *tendere*, "to stretch" \cite[tensor, Etymonline]{etymonline_tensor}. Hamilton gave it a mathematical life, using it for the length of a quaternion. The modern object had to solve Voigt's problem: a crystal's properties depend on the direction you probe them (stiffness, light, heat flow), and he needed one object to hold all those directional couplings — his "Tensoren," 1898 (\cite[Voigt, 1898]{voigt1898krystalle}). Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita then built the calculus that makes tensors work, 1900, so that the laws of geometry could be written with no privileged coordinate system — the language Einstein inherited for relativity (\cite[Ricci-Curbastro & Levi-Civita, 1900]{riccilevicivita1900}; \cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).

- **Summation convention** — Einstein's 1916 answer to the tedium of long sums in his new tensor equations: an index that appears twice is summed over and then vanishes from the page (\cite[Einstein, 1916]{einstein1916annalen}).

Two details sharpen that story. Voigt's word is not a definition of the modern tensor: he writes that he will call "die für sie charakteristischen physikalischen Grössen aber Tensoren" — the physical quantities characteristic of anisotropic crystals, "tensors" (\cite[Voigt, 1898]{voigt1898krystalle}). And Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita's 1900 memoir does not use the noun at all; it speaks of *systèmes* with covariant and contravariant components (\cite[Ricci-Curbastro & Levi-Civita, 1900]{riccilevicivita1900}; \cite[Miller: tensor]{miller_tensor}). The noun travelled from Voigt's crystallography into Einstein's relativity; the calculus came from the Italians.

> **One idea, many names.** Determinants came first (Seki 1683, Leibniz 1693), matrices were named for bookkeeping (Sylvester 1850), matrix algebra arrived in 1858 (Cayley), and tensors travelled from quaternions (Hamilton 1846) through crystallography (Voigt 1898) into relativity (Einstein 1916). The array is the modern container; the history is the set of problems it was built to hold.

The Hadamard Product ($\odot$)

The **Hadamard Product** ($\odot$) was introduced by \citeauthor{hadamardproduct} to study **singularities** in complex power series: the term-by-term product and the related **Hadamard multiplication theorem** belong to his 1899 *Acta Mathematica* paper \citetitle{hadamard1899series}. It is defined for vectors as $\vec{a} \odot \vec{b} = (a_1 b_1, \dots, a_n b_n)^T$ — the coefficients are multiplied term by term — which is exactly what lets one predict the analytic continuation and boundaries of functions derived from known ones.

The history is a little more tangled than the name suggests. Hadamard's 1892 thesis was about Taylor series and analytic continuation; the term-by-term product and its multiplication theorem belong to his 1899 *Acta Mathematica* paper (\cite[Hadamard, 1899]{hadamard1899series}). For matrices the key result is Schur's: the Hadamard product of two positive-semidefinite matrices is positive-semidefinite, proved as Theorem VII of his 1911 paper (\cite[Schur, 1911]{schur1911bilinear}). The name "Hadamard product" for the matrix operation was popularised by Paul Halmos, who recalled that John von Neumann suggested it (\cite[Hadamard product, Wikipedia]{hadamard_product_wiki}).

While standard matrix multiplication follows the “row-by-column” rule, the **Hadamard Product** (also known as the *element-wise product*) is much more straightforward. It takes two matrices or vectors of the **same dimensions** and multiplies the elements that occupy the same position.

In the context of Deep Learning, the $\odot$ symbol is ubiquitous. It is used in **Layer Normalization** to scale normalized values by a learnable parameter $\gamma$, and in **Gating Mechanisms** (like LSTMs or GRUs) to decide which information should pass through a “gate.”

Softmax and Cross-Entropy
Two vector operations appear so often in AI that they deserve explicit definitions here, even though they are first motivated in the Statistics and Loss chapters.
Softmax: vector → probability distribution
Given a vector of real-valued scores $\vec{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ (called **logits**), the **softmax** turns it into a vector of probabilities that sum to $1$:

The formula is older than machine learning. It is the **Boltzmann distribution** of statistical mechanics — Boltzmann's 1868 paper, Gibbs's textbook of 1902 — with the logits playing the role of negative energies (\cite[Boltzmann distribution]{boltzmann_distribution_wiki}). R. Duncan Luce derived it from his choice axiom in 1959 (\cite[Luce, 1959]{luce1959individualchoice}). The name "softmax" is John Bridle's; he used it for a normalised exponential in a 1989 conference paper published in 1990 (\cite[Bridle, 1990]{bridle1990softmax}).

blocks.quote: Given a true probability distribution $\vec{y}$ (one-hot for a single correct class) and a predicted distribution $\hat{\vec{y}}$ (the model's softmax output), the **cross-entropy** is
blocks.section: Cross-entropy: measuring the gap between two distributions

blocks.quote: That is: cross-entropy loss for a single example is just the **negative log-probability the model assigned to the correct class**. This is the standard classification loss (see the Loss chapter) and, paired with softmax, has the elegant property
blocks.section: Cross-entropy: measuring the gap between two distributions

blocks.quote: The $\hat{y}_i$ factors from the softmax Jacobian cancel the $1/\hat{y}_i$ factors from the cross-entropy gradient, leaving the remarkably simple "predicted minus actual" — which is precisely why softmax + cross-entropy is the canonical pairing.
